content:
The best exercise for rheumatoid arthritis is a mix: regular low-impact aerobic activity such as walking, swimming or cycling, strengthening exercises two or more days a week, and daily gentle stretches for stiff joints. Exercise does not make RA worse. It reduces pain, stiffness and fatigue and protects your heart. During a flare, scale it back rather than stopping completely.

Why exercise matters in RA

RA affects much more than joints. It increases the risk of heart disease, can cause muscle loss and often brings heavy fatigue. Regular activity helps with all of these. NICE (NG100) recommends that adults with RA have access to physiotherapy to improve fitness and encourage regular exercise.

Related reading: What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?, Chair-based exercise for rheumatoid arthritis and frailty (UK), Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment

Aerobic exercise

This is activity that makes you breathe a little faster and feel warmer.

  • walking — the easiest place to start. Try short walks most days and build up gradually.
  • swimming or water exercise — warm water eases stiffness and supports your weight
  • cycling — a static bike at home or gentle rides outdoors
  • dancing or exercise classes designed for people with joint problems

The UK Chief Medical Officers suggest aiming for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week. You can work towards this in short chunks of 10 minutes or more.

Strengthening

Stronger muscles support and protect your joints. Include strengthening on at least two days a week.

  • sit to stand from a chair
  • wall press-ups
  • step-ups on the bottom stair, holding the banister
  • resistance band exercises for shoulders, arms and legs
  • light hand weights or tins of food

Start with a weight you can lift 10 to 15 times comfortably and add more as you get stronger.

Flexibility and range of movement

Gentle stretches, ideally every day, help keep joints moving. Tai chi, yoga and Pilates can help with flexibility and balance. Tell the instructor about your RA and choose a gentle class.

Hand exercises

Hands are often affected in RA. Simple exercises include making a gentle fist, touching each fingertip to your thumb, and spreading your fingers flat on a table. An occupational therapist or hand therapist can give you a tailored programme and advise on splints.

Exercising around flares

During a flare:

  • rest inflamed joints but keep gently moving them through their range a few times a day to prevent stiffness
  • switch to gentler activity, such as short walks or water exercise
  • avoid strengthening the flaring joint until swelling settles
  • build back up gradually once the flare eases

Use the two-hour pain rule: if pain is noticeably worse two hours after exercise, do a little less next time.

Safety tips

  • warm up for five to ten minutes and cool down afterwards
  • choose supportive footwear
  • if your neck is affected by RA, avoid exercises that put pressure on the neck and tell instructors
  • if you take steroids long-term or have osteoporosis, ask about safe exercise for your bones
  • infection risk is higher on some medicines. Keep water bottles and kit clean.

Getting started

If you are new to exercise or worried about your joints, ask your rheumatology team for a physiotherapy referral, or check whether you can self-refer locally. Many leisure centres run classes for people with long-term conditions. Pick activities you enjoy, as you are more likely to keep them up.

Keeping motivated

Set small goals, such as walking to the end of the road and back each day this week. Exercise with a friend, join a class or use a simple activity tracker. Remember that the benefits of exercise build over weeks, so give it time.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
